extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political economy; economists and policy students
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of classical price theory from Adam Smith: decomposition of commodity price into rent, wages, and profit; definitions of natural and market price; the role of effectual demand and quantity brought to market in determining market price; and related monetary/coinage considerations (mint price, bullion, seignorage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of price: rent, wages, profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of most commodities finally resolves into three component parts: the rent of land, the wages of labour, and the profits of stock (the undertaker’s profit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In the price of corn one part pays rent, another wages of labour and labouring cattle, and the third pays the farmer’s profit. The price of manufactured goods adds successive wages and profits at each stage (miller, baker, miller’s and baker’s servants, etc.). The guidance emphasizes that these three parts either immediately or ultimately make up the whole price of most commodities and that all other revenue is ultimately derived from these three sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour as the measure of real value
rubrics_metrics.description: The real value of the different component parts of price is measured by the quantity of labour which they can each purchase or command; labour measures value not only of the labour-part but also of rent and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith explains that the value of rent and profit is ultimately traceable to labour, and therefore the whole price and distribution of produce among wages, profit, and rent is measured in terms of labour commanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit of stock distinct from wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits of stock are not simply wages for inspection and direction; they are regulated by the value/extent of the stock employed and bear no regular proportion to the labour of supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: Two manufactures with equal numbers of workmen and similar supervisory labour can yield very different profits if the capital employed differs (one uses materials costing seven hundred pounds, another seven thousand). The owner expects profit proportional to capital even when his supervisory labour is minimal; the clerk’s wages reflect the actual labour of direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural price (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural price of a commodity is that price which is sufficient to pay the rent of the land, the wages of labour, and the profits of the stock employed in producing and bringing it to market, each at their natural rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The natural price is described as the price at which the commodity is ‘precisely for what it is worth’ and the lowest price at which a dealer is likely to sell for any considerable time (where there is liberty to change trade). If a dealer sells below ordinary profit he is a loser compared to employing his stock elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market price (definition and relation to natural price)
rubrics_metrics.description: The market price is the actual price at which a commodity is commonly sold; it may be above, below, or equal to the natural price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The market price fluctuates around the natural price, which acts as the ‘central price’ toward which market prices gravitate. Accidents can keep prices suspended above or force them below the natural price, but they tend to return to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectual demand (vs absolute demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectual demand consists of those buyers willing and able to pay the natural price (the rent, wages, and profit required to bring the commodity to market); it is distinct from absolute demand (mere desire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A poor man may desire a coach-and-six (absolute demand) but cannot effectuate bringing such a commodity to market (not effectual demand). Market price depends on effectual demand, not mere desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market price determined by relation of quantity to effectual demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The market price is regulated by the proportion between the quantity actually brought to market and the effectual demand for the commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quantity < effectual demand, competition among buyers raises market price above natural price; when quantity > effectual demand, competition among sellers pushes market price below natural price; when quantity equals effectual demand, market price tends toward natural price. Perishability accentuates price falls when there is an excess (e.g., oranges vs old iron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural rates of wages, profit, and rent
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an ordinary or average (natural) rate of wages, profit, and rent in every society or neighbourhood, regulated partly by general circumstances of the society (riches, condition) and partly by the nature of each employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These natural rates are the benchmark used in defining the natural price; they are discussed as being shaped by social and local conditions and by the particular employment’s character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity supplied adjusts to effectual demand via self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If supply exceeds effectual demand, interests of landlords, labourers, and capitalists prompt withdrawal of resources from that employment; if supply is deficient, interests prompt increased preparation and employment—thus supply tends toward the effectual demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: landlords withdraw land (if rent depressed); labourers and employers withdraw labour or stock (if wages/profits depressed); conversely they mobilize more resources if profits or wages rise above natural rates. This self-interested adjustment returns prices toward their natural level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early/rude societies: labour-time as exchange regulator
rubrics_metrics.description: In early and rude societies (before accumulation of stock and appropriation of land), the proportion between quantities of labour necessary to acquire different objects is the main rule for exchanging them (e.g., if beaver requires twice the labour of deer, one beaver exchanges for two deer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes exceptions where severity or required skill leads to allowances (hardship or dexterity compensated), and that such allowances later appear in wages as societies advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture raises relative share of wages and profit
rubrics_metrics.description: As a commodity undergoes more stages of manufacture, the portion of its price that resolves into wages and profit increases relative to that which resolves into rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every stage adds another wage and profit; subsequent profits are often larger because the capital employing later stages must be greater (it replaces earlier capital plus pays wages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Some commodities have only two or one price components
rubrics_metrics.description: A few commodities’ price resolves into wages and profit only, and a still smaller number into wages only (e.g., sea-fish: wages and profit; Scotch pebbles gathered on shore: wages only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith uses fisheries and small gathering trades to illustrate how rent may be absent in certain commodities’ prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money price defined by quantity of pure metal, not coin denomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Money price is understood as the quantity of pure gold or silver for which goods are sold, irrespective of the denomination of the coin (e.g., six shillings and eight pence in Edward I’s time is treated as same money price as a modern pound sterling if they contain similar quantities of silver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes that monetary values should be compared by metal content (pure gold/silver), not nominal coin labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mint price vs market price of bullion and coins
rubrics_metrics.description: The mint price (quantity of coin given per weight of bullion) can diverge from the market price of bullion; reformation of coin, export permissions, and prohibitions can influence these differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and historical notes: English mint coins fifty-two? (text gives sixty-two shillings per pound weight) leading to a mint price for silver; before and after gold coin reformation, market prices of bullion fluctuated relative to mint price; Locke’s explanation (permission to export bullion and prohibition to export coin) is discussed and questioned. Smith explains that coin standards, undervaluations/overvaluations in coin, export permissions, and convenience/delay in coinage influence these divergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative rating of metals in coin versus their bullion market ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: The valuation of metals in a country’s coin (e.g., copper rated above real value, silver rated below relative to gold in English coin) can differ from their proportions in the bullion market abroad (French/Dutch ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes English coinexchange: an ounce of fine gold exchanges for about fifteen ounces of fine silver in English coin, whereas in European coin it is about fourteen. Such differences are due to coin ratings, but bullion market prices abroad remain governed by true metal proportions; copper and silver being over- or under-rated in domestic coin does not necessarily sink their bullion price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seignorage (coinage duty) raises coin value above bullion and discourages export/melting
rubrics_metrics.description: A small seignorage or duty upon coinage increases the value of metal in coin relative to bullion and thus prevents melting down and discourages exportation of coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues such a duty increases coin’s domestic superiority; gives example of France where seignorage ~8% is said to make exported French coin return of its own accord. Seignorage makes coin more valuable at home than abroad and can lead to natural importation back if exported during exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin standard accuracy and wear affect money as a measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy of money as a measure of value depends on how closely current coin conforms to its standard weight of pure metal; wear, rubbing, and uneven diminution introduce uncertainty into money prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if forty-four guineas and a half should equal a pound weight of standard gold but worn coin contains less, the merchant adjusts prices to what coin actually contains on average. Wear causes merchants to price by average coin content rather than ideal standard, producing uncertainty similar to other imperfect weights and measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience and delay in coinage make coin worth more than bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin is more convenient than bullion; delays in returning bullion to owners in coin (mint processing delays) act like a small duty, making coin somewhat more valuable than equivalent weight of bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes that free coinage notwithstanding, practical delay in converting bullion to coin (weeks or months of mint backlog) is equivalent to a small duty and renders coin more valuable. This convenience premium helps explain why coin may purchase more than its nominal bullion content.
